2015B16.goal: Al, Bill and Cal get distinct numbers from $1$ to $10$. We want the probability that Cal's number divides Bill's and Bill's divides Al's. Count divisibility chains $c\mid b\mid a$ with $c<b<a\le10$.

tools.name: Counting ordered outcomes
tools.why: Distinct numbers assigned to three named people.

tools.name: Chains by smallest element
tools.why: Systematic casework avoids misses.

2015B16.approach: Since the numbers are distinct, "multiple" means a strictly larger multiple. Count chains $c<b<a$ with $c\mid b$ and $b\mid a$, starting from $c=1$, then $c=2$, and so on.

check.q: How many multiples of $3$ greater than $3$ are at most $10$?
Why is there no chain starting at $c=3$?

2015B16.bridge: Count chains $c\mid b\mid a$ by the smallest number and divide by $720$.
2015B16.shortcut: Every chain is determined by its numbers, and each set appears in exactly one valid order.
traps: Allowing equal numbers.
Dividing by $1000$ instead of $720$.
2015B16.recognize: Probability of a divisibility chain among distinct picks: count chains by smallest element.

2015B17.goal: Joining the centres of the six faces of a $3\times4\times5$ box makes an octahedron. We want its volume. The octahedron is two pyramids glued along a rhombus.

tools.name: Rhombus area
tools.why: Half the product of the diagonals.

tools.name: Pyramid volume
tools.why: Standard formula.

2015B17.approach: The four side-face centres form a rhombus in the middle horizontal plane with diagonals equal to the box's length and width. The top and bottom face centres are apexes at height $\tfrac h2$ above and below. Add the two pyramids.

steps.title: The middle rhombus
steps.explain: The four side-face centres are midpoints of the box's middle cross-section, a rhombus with diagonals $a$ and $b$ (the two horizontal dimensions). Area $\tfrac12ab$.

check.q: A rhombus has diagonals $4$ and $5$. What is its area?

steps.title: Two pyramids
steps.explain: Each pyramid has height $\tfrac c2$, so the volume is $2\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12ab\cdot\tfrac c2=\tfrac{abc}{6}$. For $3\times4\times5$: $\tfrac{60}6=10$.

2015B17.bridge: Split the octahedron into two pyramids on the middle rhombus.
solution: The middle rhombus has diagonals equal to two box dimensions: area $\tfrac12ab$.
Two pyramids of height $\tfrac c2$: volume $\tfrac{abc}{6}$.
2015B17.shortcut: The face-centre octahedron of any box has volume $\tfrac16$ of the box.
traps: Treating it as a regular octahedron.
Using full height $c$ for each pyramid.
2015B17.recognize: Solids formed by face centres: decompose into pyramids whose bases are cross-sections.

2015B18.goal: Each of $64$ coins is tossed up to three times, stopping at heads. We want the expected number of heads at the end. Linearity of expectation lets us handle one coin and multiply.

tools.name: Linearity of expectation
tools.why: Expectation adds even without independence.

tools.name: Complement
tools.why: A coin ends tails only if all three tosses are tails.

2015B18.approach: One coin ends as heads unless it is tails three times. Multiply that probability by $64$.

check.q: With up to $2$ tosses, what is $P(\text{heads at the end})$?

2015B18.bridge: Find one coin's probability of ending heads and multiply by $64$.
solution: A coin ends tails only if it is tails on all three tosses: $\tfrac18$.
So each coin is heads with probability $\tfrac78$.
2015B18.shortcut: Expected value of a count = number of items $\times$ probability for one item.
traps: Adding $32+16+8$ and forgetting it equals $56$ only by coincidence of method.
Thinking the tosses must be simulated round by round.
2015B18.recognize: Expected counts: use linearity and compute the probability for a single item.

2015B19.goal: Right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $C$, $AB=12$) has squares on $AB$ and $AC$, and the four outer corners $X,Y,Z,W$ lie on a circle. We want the perimeter. The concyclic condition forces the triangle to be isosceles.

tools.name: Centre of a circle through a chord
tools.fact: \text{centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of every chord}
tools.why: It is equidistant from the chord's ends.

tools.name: Circumcentre of a right triangle
tools.why: Thales: the hypotenuse is a diameter.

tools.name: Distance formula
tools.why: Pythagoras in coordinates.

2015B19.approach: $XY\parallel AB$ and $ZW\parallel AC$ share perpendicular bisectors with $AB$ and $AC$. These meet at the circumcentre of $ABC$, the midpoint $M$ of $AB$. So $MX=MZ$; express both with legs $a,b$ and solve.

steps.title: Locate the centre
steps.explain: The perpendicular bisector of $XY$ is that of $AB$; of $ZW$ is that of $AC$. They meet at the circumcentre of $ABC$, which is $M$, the midpoint of $AB$.

check.q: Where is the circumcentre of a right triangle?

steps.title: Perimeter
steps.explain: Isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse $12$: legs $6\sqrt2$. Perimeter $12+12\sqrt2$.

check.q: Legs of an isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse $12$?

2015B19.bridge: Find the circle's centre as the midpoint of $AB$, set $MX=MZ$, and solve.
solution: The circle's centre is on the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$, so it is the midpoint $M$ of $AB$.
2015B19.shortcut: Symmetry suggests the isosceles case; the algebra confirms it is the only one.
traps: Assuming a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle.
Placing the squares inside the triangle.
2015B19.recognize: Concyclic points built from squares on sides: perpendicular bisectors locate the centre; equate distances.

2015B20.goal: Erin walks $7$ edges on a cube, visiting all $8$ corners once, and cannot return to the start. We count such paths. Colouring corners in two alternating colours decides where she can end.

tools.name: Bipartite colouring
tools.fact: \text{Each edge joins corners of opposite colours}
tools.why: Colour by the parity of the number of $1$s in coordinates $(x,y,z)\in\{0,1\}^3$.

tools.name: Where a 7-step path ends
tools.fact: \text{after }7\text{ steps the colour has flipped: distance }1\text{ or }3
tools.why: Odd steps change colour; corners of the other colour are the $3$ neighbours and the opposite corner.

2015B20.approach: "Cannot return along an edge" means the end is not adjacent to the start. By colouring, the end must be the opposite corner. Count paths from a corner to the opposite corner visiting every corner.

steps.title: Where she ends
steps.explain: After $7$ edges she is on the opposite colour: a neighbour of the start or the opposite corner. Not a neighbour, so the opposite corner.

check.q: How many corners of a cube are at distance $3$ from a given corner?

steps.title: Count the paths
steps.explain: First edge: $3$ choices. Second edge: $2$ choices (not back). After that the route is forced: she must save the opposite corner for last. Checking one case: $000\to100\to110\to010\to011\to001\to101\to111$. So $3\cdot2=6$ paths.

2015B20.bridge: Use the colouring to show she ends opposite, then count with the first two choices.
solution: A $7$-edge path flips colour, so it ends at a neighbour or the opposite corner; not a neighbour, so opposite.
Choose the first edge ($3$) and second edge ($2$); the rest is forced.
2015B20.shortcut: Of the $18$ paths through all corners from a fixed start, $12$ end next to it; $18-12=6$.
traps: Counting all $18$ paths.
Forgetting that the end must be the opposite corner.
2015B20.recognize: Paths on grids and cubes: two-colour the vertices to restrict where a path of given length can end.

2015B21.goal: Cozy needs $\lceil\tfrac n2\rceil$ jumps and Dash $\lceil\tfrac n5\rceil$ for $n$ steps; Dash takes $19$ fewer. We find all $n$ and the digit sum of their total.

tools.name: Ceiling for jump counts
tools.why: The last partial jump still counts.

tools.name: Estimate then check
tools.why: Ceilings change the difference by at most about $1$.

2015B21.approach: Estimate $n$ from $\tfrac{3n}{10}\approx19$, then check a small range of $n$ around $63$ directly.
2015B21.bridge: Estimate $n$ and test nearby values with ceilings.
2015B21.shortcut: The difference grows by about $0.3$ per step, so only a few $n$ near $63$ can work.
traps: Using floor instead of ceiling.
Missing $n=66$.
2015B21.recognize: Equations with ceilings or floors of linear expressions: estimate with the real-number version, then check a narrow window.

2015B22.goal: In a regular pentagon with its star of diagonals, $AG=1$ is a side of one of the star's points. We want $FG+JH+CD$. Every length in a regular pentagram is one of a few values related by the golden ratio $\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$.

tools.name: Golden ratio
tools.why: It satisfies $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$.

tools.name: Lengths in a regular pentagram
tools.why: Similar isosceles $36^\circ$-$72^\circ$-$72^\circ$ triangles appear throughout the figure.

2015B22.approach: Take the star-point side $AG=1$ as the unit. Then an inner pentagon side is $\tfrac1\varphi=\varphi-1$ and an outer pentagon side is $1+(\varphi-1)=\varphi$. In the figure, $FG$ is an inner side, $JH$ is a star-point side (like $AG$), and $CD$ is an outer side.

steps.title: The three lengths
steps.explain: A star point is a golden triangle with legs $1$ and base equal to the inner side, $\tfrac1\varphi=\varphi-1$. The outer side is a star-point leg plus an inner side: $\varphi$.

2015B22.bridge: Express each segment as a star-point side, inner side, or outer side, using $\varphi$.
solution: With $AG=1$ (a star-point side), inner pentagon sides are $\varphi-1$ and outer sides are $\varphi$.
$FG$ is an inner side, $JH$ a star-point side, $CD$ an outer side.
2015B22.shortcut: Every pentagram length is a power of $\varphi$ times the smallest piece; identify each piece's type.
traps: Treating all star segments as equal.
Using $\varphi=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}2$ (that is $\tfrac1\varphi$).
2015B22.recognize: Regular pentagons and pentagrams: golden-ratio relationships from similar $36^\circ$-$72^\circ$-$72^\circ$ triangles.

2015B23.goal: $n!$ ends in $k$ zeros and $(2n)!$ in $3k$ zeros. We want the four smallest $n>4$ and the digit sum of their total. Count zeros with factors of $5$.

tools.name: Trailing zeros of a factorial
tools.why: Each zero needs a factor $10$; fives are scarcer than twos.

2015B23.approach: Doubling $n$ roughly doubles the zero count, so $3k$ needs the jumps at multiples of $5$ to line up favourably. Check $n=5,6,\ldots$ until four work.
2015B23.bridge: Compute $Z(n)$ and $Z(2n)$ for successive $n$ and collect the first four matches.
2015B23.shortcut: $2n$ must reach $25$ (extra five) while $n$ stays just below a multiple of $5$; that explains $13,14$.
traps: Forgetting the extra factor from $25$.
Including $n\le4$.
2015B23.recognize: Trailing zeros of factorials: count fives (Legendre's formula) and test small cases.

2015B24.goal: Aaron walks a square spiral starting east. We want $p_{2015}$. Find a pattern for the corners of the spiral, then walk the last few steps.

tools.name: Run lengths
tools.why: Side lengths of the spiral grow by $1$ every turn.

2015B24.approach: Spiral side lengths are $1,1,2,2,3,3,\ldots$, so corners occur at $k(k+1)$. Find the largest $k(k+1)\le2015$, locate that corner, and move the remaining steps in the correct direction.

steps.title: Walk the rest
steps.explain: From the lower-left corner he walks east for $45$ steps. $2015-1980=35$ steps east: $(-22+35,-22)=(13,-22)$.

2015B24.bridge: Locate the corner $p_{1980}$ and walk $35$ steps east.
2015B24.shortcut: Verify the corner formula on the first few points before trusting it.
traps: Using $45^2=2025$ (squares are not the corners here).
Walking north instead of east after the lower-left corner.
2015B24.recognize: Spiral walks: side lengths $1,1,2,2,3,3,\ldots$ make corners at $k(k+1)$; find the nearest corner and walk.

2015B25.goal: Integer boxes $a\le b\le c$ with volume equal to surface area: $abc=2(ab+bc+ca)$. Dividing by $abc$ gives $\tfrac1a+\tfrac1b+\tfrac1c=\tfrac12$. We count solutions.

tools.name: Unit fraction form
tools.why: Divide both sides by $abc$.

tools.name: Bounding the smallest
tools.why: $a$ is the smallest, so $\tfrac1a$ is the largest term.

tools.name: Simon's trick
tools.why: Clear denominators and factor.

2015B25.approach: Bound $a$ between $3$ and $6$. For each $a$, solve $\tfrac1b+\tfrac1c=\tfrac12-\tfrac1a$ by factoring, counting pairs with $a\le b\le c$.
2015B25.bridge: Rewrite as unit fractions, bound $a$, and factor for each $a$.
2015B25.shortcut: Unit fraction equations always bound the smallest variable first.
traps: Forgetting $b\ge a$.
Counting ordered triples without $a\le b\le c$.
2015B25.recognize: "Volume equals surface area" and similar: divide to get unit fractions, then bound and factor.
